name: Minishell
description: A POSIX-compliant Unix shell written in C from scratch, with a full lexer-parser-executor pipeline, pipes, redirections, and built-in commands.

terminal.caption: A session from the project's own screenshot, typed out as text.

overview: Minishell is a Unix shell implemented from scratch in C as part of the 42 Prague curriculum, built with a partner under strict coding standards. It reproduces core Bash behavior end to end: an interactive prompt with command history via GNU Readline, a lexer and parser that turn raw input into an executable command structure, environment variable expansion, and a process-based executor that runs built-ins and external binaries.
architecture: The codebase is split into a lexer/parser/expander pipeline (lexer.c, lexer_token.c, lexer_extract.c, parser.c, parser_utils.c, expander.c, expander_utils.c) that turns raw input into a structured command list, and an execution layer (executor.c, executor_utils.c, path_finder.c, redirections.c, heredoc.c, wait.c) that forks processes, wires up pipes and file descriptors, and waits on children. Built-in commands run in-process rather than being forked, and a dedicated environment layer (env.c, env_utils.c) manages the shell's variable list independently of the OS environment array. A custom libft utility library backs the string and memory helpers used throughout.
keyFeatures: Interactive prompt with command history via GNU Readline
Lexer and parser that tokenize and structure raw input, including quote handling
Pipelines (|) and multi-command chaining through process creation
Redirections (<, >, >>) and heredocs (<<) with delimiter support
Built-in commands: echo, cd, pwd, env, export, unset, exit
Environment variable ($VAR) expansion with an independently managed environment list
Signal handling that adapts to interactive mode, heredoc input, and child execution
challenges: Reproducing Bash-like parsing and expansion behavior without access to Bash's own source or internal state
Managing file descriptors and process lifetimes correctly across pipelines, redirections, and heredocs so nothing leaked or closed early
Handling signals differently depending on shell state: interactive prompt, heredoc input, or a running child process
engineeringDecisions: Separated the shell's environment state (env.c) from the OS environment array so built-ins like export and unset can mutate it without exec() side effects
Kept built-ins running in the parent process instead of forking, since commands like cd and export must affect the shell's own state, not a child's
Split lexing, parsing, and expansion into distinct passes instead of one large parser function, making quote handling and $VAR expansion easier to reason about and test in isolation
technologyNotes: Written in C targeting Linux/Unix, using POSIX system calls (fork, execve, waitpid, dup2, pipe) for process and file-descriptor control, GNU Readline for interactive input and history, and a custom libft utility library for string and memory helpers.
lessonsLearned: Strengthened low-level debugging skills using gdb and Valgrind to track down descriptor leaks and memory issues
Learned to validate shell behavior empirically against real Bash rather than assumptions
Practiced Git-based collaboration on a shared, peer-reviewed C codebase under strict coding-standard constraints

name: faresm.dev
description: This site: ASP.NET Core 10 with server-rendered pages and a REST API over the same JSON-backed data, deployed to Azure App Service by GitHub Actions using OIDC, with no publish profile or client secret stored.
overview: The site you are reading. It started as a static page that fetched JSON in the browser and was rebuilt so the server does the work: every page is rendered with Razor Pages from the same data service that backs a small REST API, so crawlers, link previews and visitors without JavaScript get complete HTML. It runs on Azure App Service at faresm.dev over HTTPS, and every push to main goes through an automated build, test and deploy pipeline.
architecture: Content lives in two JSON files (profile and projects) outside the web root. A singleton data service reads them, caches the parsed result in memory and evicts it when a file changes. Razor Pages render the home page and one detail page per project from that service, while API controllers expose the same data at /api/profile and /api/projects. A media service discovers screenshot folders on disk and reads image dimensions from file headers, so every image ships with explicit width and height. Deployment is a two-job GitHub Actions workflow: the build job builds the app, runs the xUnit test suite and publishes an artifact; the deploy job signs in to Azure with OpenID Connect and deploys that artifact to App Service.
keyFeatures: Server-rendered pages: complete HTML for crawlers, link previews and visitors without JavaScript
REST endpoints (/api/profile, /api/projects, /api/projects/{slug}) backed by the same data service as the pages
Real 404 responses for unknown routes and project slugs
Screenshot galleries discovered from the filesystem, with image dimensions read from file headers
xUnit integration tests (WebApplicationFactory) that run in CI before every deploy
Deployment authenticated with OIDC federated credentials instead of a stored publish profile or client secret
Custom domain (faresm.dev) served over HTTPS with HSTS
challenges: Moving from client-side to server-side rendering without changing the JSON API or the data format behind it
Making sure the content files are only reachable through the API and the pages, not downloadable as raw static files
Deploying to Azure from CI without keeping long-lived credentials in the repository
engineeringDecisions: Rendered pages on the server with Razor Pages instead of adding a frontend framework, keeping JavaScript for progressive enhancement only
Kept content in JSON files rather than a database, since it is small, changes rarely and is edited by hand; an in-memory cache with file-change invalidation keeps reads cheap
Used OIDC federated credentials for the Azure login, so the workflow exchanges a short-lived GitHub token for Azure access instead of storing a deploy password
Read image dimensions from file headers instead of adding an imaging library dependency
technologyNotes: C# on ASP.NET Core 10 (Razor Pages and API controllers), vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS on the front end, xUnit with WebApplicationFactory for tests, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and Azure App Service for hosting.
lessonsLearned: When the content already lives on the server, server-side rendering is the simplest fix for SEO and link previews
Federated identity removes the need to store and rotate a deploy secret in CI/CD
Integration tests against the real HTTP pipeline catch routing and status-code regressions that unit tests miss

name: AI Job Search Assistant
description: A local, Docker-based job-search automation system that aggregates listings from multiple sources, filters and scores them, removes duplicates, and tracks applications in Google Sheets.
overview: A local, Docker-based job-search automation system that aggregates job listings from multiple sources, filters and scores them, removes duplicates, and tracks applications in Google Sheets. It is a personal project and runs locally in Docker.
architecture: n8n orchestrates Python/FastAPI services running in Docker. The workflow pulls listings through a JobSpy integration and a dedicated Jobs.cz scraping service, scores their relevance with an LLM, and writes the results to Google Sheets, where applications are tracked.
keyFeatures: Multi-source job search
JobSpy integration
Dedicated Jobs.cz scraping service
Job deduplication
Location and relevance filtering
LLM-based relevance scoring
Google Sheets read/write for application tracking
Local service orchestration with Docker
technologyNotes: Python and FastAPI for the services, n8n for workflow orchestration, Docker to run the services locally, the Google Sheets API for application tracking, and an LLM for relevance scoring, connected through REST APIs and JSON.

name: Hotel Booking Database
description: A normalized PostgreSQL database for hotel booking management, with trigger-driven price recalculation and automatic booking-status transitions.
overview: A relational database system for managing bookings across multiple hotels, designed from a conceptual ER model through to a working PostgreSQL schema. It models hotels, rooms with per-room bed configurations, customers, price plans, multi-room bookings, payments, and hotel-specific extra services, with the schema itself, not just application code, responsible for keeping booking totals, room counts, and booking status correct as data changes.
architecture: The schema is organized around 13 tables in third normal form, connected through primary and composite foreign-key relationships, for example Room is keyed by (hotel_id, number) and referenced compositely by Beds_in_room and Booking_item. Business logic that needs to run no matter which client touches the data, total price calculation, booking-status transitions, and service-usage validation, is implemented as PL/pgSQL functions and triggers rather than left to application code, so the database itself enforces consistency.
keyFeatures: Multi-hotel, multi-room bookings with per-room bed-type configuration
Automatic booking total-price recalculation via triggers whenever booking items or extra services are inserted, updated, or deleted
Automatic booking-status transitions driven by payment events
CHECK-constraint-enforced business rules: positive prices, valid check-in/check-out ranges, adult-only customers, 1-5 star ratings
Flexible price plans and hotel-specific extra services with optional per-booking usage limits
Payment tracking across multiple methods and statuses (pending, succeed, failed, refunded, under review)
20+ SQL queries covering joins, aggregations and subqueries
challenges: Keeping a booking's total price correct automatically as its rooms and extra services change, without relying on the application layer to recompute it
Modeling composite relationships correctly, since rooms are identified by hotel plus room number rather than a single surrogate key, across every dependent table
Writing set-based queries, such as customers with confirmed bookings or bookings using every extra service a hotel offers, using correlated subqueries and set operators instead of procedural loops
engineeringDecisions: Pushed price and status consistency into PL/pgSQL functions and triggers instead of application code, so the guarantee holds no matter what inserts or updates the data
Used composite foreign keys (hotel_id, room_number) rather than a synthetic room ID, since a room only makes sense in the context of its hotel
Modeled extra services and their usage limits per hotel rather than globally, since two hotels can define the same service differently
technologyNotes: PostgreSQL as the database engine, with the schema, constraints, and business logic written directly in SQL and PL/pgSQL rather than an ORM, to practice relational modeling and set-based query writing directly.
lessonsLearned: Deepened understanding of relational modeling and normalization beyond textbook examples, including when composite keys are the right choice
Learned to express business rules as constraints and triggers so the schema stays correct independent of the application
Practiced writing SQL well beyond basic CRUD: correlated subqueries, EXISTS/NOT EXISTS, and set operators like EXCEPT

name: Philosophers
description: A multithreaded C simulation of the Dining Philosophers problem, using POSIX threads and mutexes to prevent deadlocks while enforcing strict timing constraints.

terminal.caption: Real output from building and running the public repo.

lines.text:
0 1 has taken a fork
0 1 has taken a fork
0 1 is eating
0 3 has taken a fork
0 3 has taken a fork
0 3 is eating
200 4 has taken a fork
200 4 has taken a fork
200 4 is eating
200 2 has taken a fork
200 2 has taken a fork
200 2 is eating

overview: An implementation of the classic Dining Philosophers concurrency problem in C using POSIX threads, where each philosopher runs as its own thread alternating between thinking, eating, and sleeping while sharing a fixed number of forks with its neighbors. The simulation enforces strict timing rules, a philosopher who doesn't eat before a configurable time-to-die limit is detected as dead, so correctness depends as much on precise timing as on avoiding deadlocks and race conditions.
architecture: Each philosopher runs on its own pthread executing a shared routine that cycles through thinking, taking two fork mutexes, eating, releasing them, and sleeping. A separate monitor thread runs concurrently, checking every philosopher's last-meal timestamp against the time-to-die limit to detect starvation without interrupting the eating threads. A dedicated timing helper breaks sleep calls into short intervals so the monitor can still detect a death promptly instead of oversleeping past the deadline.
keyFeatures: Independent philosopher threads synchronized with per-fork mutexes to prevent two neighbors eating with the same fork at once
Dedicated monitor thread that detects philosopher death based on a configurable time-to-die limit
Optional meal-count limit so the simulation can end once every philosopher has eaten enough times
Millisecond-precision timing via a custom sleep helper to avoid missing the death deadline
challenges: Preventing deadlock when every philosopher tries to pick up forks at once, without serializing them so heavily that the simulation stops behaving concurrently
Detecting a philosopher's death within the required timing precision without a busy-wait loop burning CPU or a long sleep call missing the deadline
Protecting shared state, last meal time and the death flag, from race conditions between each philosopher thread and the monitor thread
engineeringDecisions: Used a dedicated monitor thread instead of having each philosopher check its own death condition, since a philosopher blocked waiting for a fork can't reliably watch its own clock
Broke long sleeps into short intervals rather than a single sleep call, trading a small amount of CPU overhead for the timing precision the monitor depends on
Guarded shared timing state with mutexes rather than atomics, keeping the synchronization model consistent with the rest of the fork-locking design
technologyNotes: C with POSIX threads (pthread) and mutexes for concurrency, built and tested on Linux.
lessonsLearned: Built a practical understanding of thread synchronization and the classic deadlock/starvation trade-offs beyond the textbook description
Learned how much correctness in a real-time-constrained concurrent system depends on timing precision, not just locking correctness
Practiced isolating shared mutable state and reasoning carefully about which thread is allowed to touch it and when

name: Business Inventory Management
description: A C# WinForms desktop application for managing products, customers, and orders for a small business, with local persistence and a live business-stats dashboard.
overview: A Windows desktop application built with C# and WinForms for managing the day-to-day inventory operations of a small business, tracking products, customers, and orders behind a login-protected interface. The home dashboard surfaces live business stats, delivered versus undelivered orders and monthly profit, plus upcoming deliveries, and a dedicated reporting view lets the user review stored records.
architecture: The application follows an event-driven WinForms structure with a login screen gating access to the main dashboard, and a sidebar-navigated interface (Home, Products, Customers, Orders, Reports) built from separate, modular forms per business area. Rather than a database engine, application state is persisted locally as JSON under the user's Windows AppData folder, created automatically on first run, keeping the application self-contained with no external server dependency.
keyFeatures: Login-protected access with a change-password flow
Product, customer, and order management: add, edit, delete, view
Home dashboard with live business statistics: delivered/undelivered orders and monthly profit
Upcoming-deliveries view for the current month
Reporting screen for reviewing stored business data
Fully local, offline data persistence with no server or internet connection required
challenges: Keeping inventory quantities, order status, and computed stats like monthly profit consistent as products, customers, and orders are added, edited, or deleted independently
Structuring the local data layer so it survives application restarts without a database engine, while staying predictable to read and write from multiple forms
engineeringDecisions: Separated the UI event handlers in each WinForms form from the underlying business logic and data-access code, so operations like computing monthly profit aren't duplicated across screens
Stored data locally under the OS-managed AppData directory instead of a bundled database file, matching how small single-user Windows desktop tools are typically distributed
technologyNotes: C# and Windows Forms (.NET) for the desktop UI and event-driven application logic, with local JSON files used for persistence instead of a database engine, keeping the application self-contained and easy to distribute as a single executable.
lessonsLearned: Practiced separating UI event handling from reusable business logic in a WinForms application
Gained experience with event-driven desktop application design end to end, from login to reporting
Learned how early persistence decisions, flat local files versus a database, shape how much rework is needed as an application grows

name: fract-ol
description: An interactive C fractal renderer for the Mandelbrot and Julia sets, with real-time zoom and colored iteration rendering built on MiniLibX.
overview: A graphical C program that renders the Mandelbrot and Julia sets interactively, using MiniLibX only for window creation and input events. All fractal math, zooming, panning, and coloring is implemented directly in program logic rather than relying on a graphics library's built-ins. The program supports both macOS and Linux by bundling platform-specific MiniLibX backends.
architecture: The code is organized by responsibility: argument parsing and validation select the fractal type and, for Julia, the complex seed; a shared iteration module implements the escape-time algorithm used by both fractals; a color module maps iteration counts to pixel colors; a render module draws the resulting frame; and an event-hook module wires up MiniLibX input (mouse scroll, keyboard, clicks) to trigger recomputation and redraw. A custom libftprintf utility library is used for formatted output.
keyFeatures: Mandelbrot and Julia set rendering from a shared iteration engine
Smooth real-time zooming via mouse scroll or +/- keys
Adjustable Julia seed values passed as command-line arguments
Mouse-click reset back to the initial view
Cross-platform support for Linux (X11) and macOS via bundled MiniLibX backends
challenges: Keeping zooming and panning responsive by recomputing only what's needed rather than the whole image on every frame, since the escape-time calculation is inherently per-pixel and CPU-bound
Supporting both Linux and macOS from the same codebase, given their different MiniLibX implementations, X11-based on Linux versus OpenGL-based on macOS
engineeringDecisions: Shared a single iteration function between the Mandelbrot and Julia renderers, since both are the same escape-time algorithm with a different starting condition, instead of duplicating the math
Kept MiniLibX strictly to window and event handling and did all rendering logic in program code, to stay in control of performance and correctness rather than relying on library internals
technologyNotes: C with MiniLibX for windowing and event handling on both Linux (X11) and macOS, plus a custom libft-style printf implementation for output.
lessonsLearned: Practiced translating a mathematical algorithm, complex-plane escape-time iteration, into an efficient, interactive rendering loop
Gained experience handling low-level input events directly through a C graphics library
Learned to write portable C across two different graphics backends behind the same interface

name: push_swap
description: A stack-sorting program in C that sorts integers with a constrained instruction set, choosing moves via a cost-based algorithm to minimize total operations.

terminal.caption: Real output from building and running the public repo.

lines.text:
pb
pb
ra
pa
pa
ra

overview: push_swap sorts an arbitrary list of integers into ascending order using only a small, constrained set of stack operations, push, swap, rotate, and reverse-rotate, across two stacks, aiming to do it in as few operations as possible rather than just correctly. Instead of a simple sort-then-translate approach, it uses a cost-based algorithm that picks the cheapest next move at every step.
architecture: The program validates and parses its integer arguments before splitting the sorting logic across dedicated modules for the primitive stack operations, composite moves, and the core target-selection and cost-calculation loop, all driven from a single entry point. Formatted output uses a custom libftprintf implementation.
keyFeatures: Sorts any valid list of integers using only the allowed stack operations (pa, pb, sa, sb, ra, rb, rra, rrb, rrr)
Cost-based move selection: computes the cheapest combination of rotations on both stacks before choosing which value to move next
Input validation rejecting non-numeric input, duplicates, and out-of-range values with a clear error
Small-stack fast path that sorts the last two or three remaining elements directly instead of running the full algorithm on them
challenges: Minimizing the total number of operations rather than just producing a correct order, which meant designing a cost model instead of picking any sorting algorithm
Deciding, for every element, the cheapest combination of same-direction rotations versus split rotations across two stacks at once
engineeringDecisions: Chose a target-node strategy, where each value is assigned the closest valid position in the sorted stack, over a generic comparison sort, since the operation-count constraint rewards moves that place a value correctly on the first try
Iterated through more than one sorting approach during development before arriving at the final cost-based algorithm
technologyNotes: C, implementing the algorithm and stack operations from scratch with no external sorting libraries, verified against the 42 curriculum's checker tool for correctness and move count.
lessonsLearned: Practiced algorithmic thinking under a hard operation-count constraint, not just correctness
Learned to reason about combined cost across two coupled data structures instead of optimizing each in isolation
Improved comfort iterating on an algorithm's design once a first working version already exists

name: Expense Tracker
description: A command-line expense and wallet tracker in Python with category, date, and amount filtering and local JSON persistence.

overview: A menu-driven command-line application for tracking personal expenses and income, and computing the resulting wallet balance from both histories. It supports filtering expense and income records by date, category, and amount, and persists all data to a local JSON file so history survives between runs.
architecture: The application is organized around an object-oriented model of expenses, income, and the wallet, with expense and income histories tracked separately and the wallet balance derived from both rather than stored as an independent value. All state loads from and saves to a single local JSON file.
keyFeatures: Add and remove individual expense and income entries
View full expense and income history
Filter expenses by amount, category, or date, and income by amount or date
Automatic wallet balance calculation from combined expense and income history
Input validation on entered amounts, categories, and dates
Persistent local storage via a JSON save file
challenges: Keeping the wallet balance correct and consistently derived from two separately tracked histories instead of letting it drift out of sync
Designing multi-criteria filtering by date, category, and amount over a plain list of records without a database query layer
engineeringDecisions: Kept expenses and income as two distinct histories rather than one combined ledger, since they're filtered and displayed differently, and derived the balance from both instead of storing it separately

Chose JSON file storage over a database for a project at this scale, while recognizing in hindsight that splitting the single-file script into separate modules and moving to SQLite would be the right next step for maintainability
technologyNotes: Python, using the standard library's json module for persistence and datetime for date handling and filtering, with no external dependencies.
lessonsLearned: Practiced core object-oriented programming and organizing a larger Python program than a single script
Learned practical JSON read/write persistence and date/time handling
Recognized in retrospect that a single-file structure limits maintainability, which now informs how later projects are split into modules from the start

name: miniGPT
description: A local LLaMA3 chatbot that runs entirely offline through Ollama, with an automated setup script and in-session conversation memory.

terminal.caption: Real run of the public repo against a local Ollama llama3 model. Blank lines are left out, and the model's replies differ between runs.

lines.text:

------------------------------
Type 'exit' to quit

lines.text:
AI >
You asked me what a Unix shell does in one sentence.
------------------------------

overview: A lightweight command-line chatbot that runs a local LLaMA3 model through Ollama, with no cloud API or external service involved. A companion setup script automates the local environment end to end, installing missing Python dependencies, installing and starting Ollama if it isn't already running, pulling the LLaMA3 model, and launching the chat loop, so the whole thing works from a single command.
architecture: The project is split into two scripts with a clear separation of concerns: one script handles environment setup, checking for and installing Python dependencies and Ollama, starting the Ollama server, and pulling the llama3 model, before launching the chatbot; the other owns the conversation loop itself, sending each user message plus the running message history to Ollama's local /api/chat endpoint and appending both the user and assistant turns to an in-memory list so the model has conversation context on each request.
keyFeatures: Fully local inference through Ollama's LLaMA3 model, no API keys, no cloud calls
One-command automated setup that installs Python dependencies and Ollama, pulls the model, and starts the chat loop
Conversation memory maintained for the duration of the session so follow-up questions have context
challenges: Automating a working local LLM environment from zero, detecting whether Ollama and the model are already installed, and installing them without user intervention when they aren't
engineeringDecisions: Kept conversation history in a simple in-memory list scoped to the session rather than persisting it to disk, since the project's goal was a minimal, fully local chat loop rather than a chat-history product
Called Ollama's REST API directly with the requests library instead of adding an SDK dependency, keeping the script's only external dependency small
technologyNotes: Python for the chatbot and setup automation, calling Ollama's local REST API to run the LLaMA3 model entirely on-device.
lessonsLearned: Practiced integrating with a local LLM runtime over HTTP instead of a hosted API
Learned to script cross-environment setup automation, dependency checks and conditional installs, so a project works out of the box on a clean machine
